Ethics is precisely the discipline that prepares us for hard cases, for the moments when ordinary rules strain against extraordinary circumstances. A moral system that can only handle easy situations is not a moral system at all.

History records numerous instances where the conditions described were tragically real. The 1972 Andes flight disaster, in which survivors of the crash of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 consumed the bodies of deceased passengers after more than two weeks without food and with no realistic prospect of rescue, stands as perhaps the most documented case. The 1846-1847 Donner Party tragedy, in which stranded pioneers resorted to consuming the dead after being snowbound in the Sierra Nevada, provides another. The Siege of Leningrad, in which the starving population of the city resorted to extreme measures during a nearly 90-day Nazi blockade, represents a case where the prohibition against cannibalism collided with mass death on an industrial scale. In each case, the common elements are exhaustion of all other resources, certainty of death without the act, and — in the morally defensible subset — consumption of those already deceased.

What is remarkable about surviving accounts is the moral anguish that accompanies the act. The Andes survivors — young men, many of them devout Catholics — described the decision to consume their friends' bodies as the most difficult moment of their ordeal, and many explicitly framed it in sacramental language, drawing parallels to the Christian Eucharist. Their anguish itself testifies to their moral seriousness: they were not people who treated the taboo lightly. The fact that they struggled with the choice, that they wept and prayed and argued among themselves for days before acting, is evidence enough that they understood the gravity of what they were doing. A further moral consideration that strengthens the case is the question of what the deceased would have wished. If a person who is dying in a survival situation explicitly or implicitly consents to their body being used to sustain others — or, as is often reported in historical cases, makes the request themselves before death — then the moral act of consumption becomes an act of fulfilling a dying person's final wish.

This argument extends further when we consider that most people, when asked hypothetically, indicate they would want their body to be used to save their companions' lives if no other option existed. Polls and thought experiments consistently show that individuals express willingness to allow postmortem consumption in survival scenarios, even if the act itself disturbs them. If autonomy is a genuine moral value — and it is foundational to liberal ethics, medical ethics, and most modern moral frameworks — then honoring a person's known or reasonably presumed wishes about the use of their body after death is a genuine moral good, not merely a permissible act.

Even absent explicit consent, we can invoke the principle of presumed consent: rational agents, understanding their own mortality and the value they place on their companions' survival, would consent to this use of their remains. This is the same logic underlying presumed-consent organ donation systems in many European countries, and it rests on a reasonable judgment about what people generally want rather than on what any specific person has said.

V. The Universalisability Test

Kant's categorical imperative demands that we act only on maxims that we could will to become universal laws. At first glance, "eat human flesh" might seem to fail this test spectacularly. But the maxim must be stated with appropriate specificity. The relevant maxim is not "eat human flesh" but rather "when facing certain death with no other means of survival, a person may consume the already-deceased to preserve their own life." Can this be universalized?

Yes. A world in which people, when facing the most extreme possible survival situation, are permitted to consume tissue from the already-deceased to stay alive is a world that no rational person would object to inhabiting. No one knows whether they will be the person trapped in the mine, stranded in the Andes, or lost at sea. Behind John Rawls's "veil of ignorance," where we choose moral rules without knowing our circumstances, any rational agent would choose a moral system that permitted survival cannibalism under strict conditions — because they might be the one whose life depends on it, and no one would choose a system that required them to die of starvation when a non-harmful alternative existed. The fact that this alternative involves cannibalism is, behind the veil, irrelevant — what matters is survival.

VI. The False Analogy of Civilization and Taboo

Perhaps the most common objection to survival cannibalism relies on the social function of the taboo itself. In many cultures, the prohibition against cannibalism serves as a foundational boundary: the line that separates civilization from barbarism, persons from things, the sacred from the profane. To violate this boundary, the argument goes, is to unravel the very fabric of moral community.

This argument confuses the general rule with the extraordinary exception. Acknowledging that cannibalism is justified in survival situations does not destabilize the taboo in normal conditions any more than acknowledging that killing in self-defense is justified destabilizes the prohibition against murder. Every moral system makes exceptions for extreme circumstances, and the existence of exceptions does not undermine the rule — it refines it. We do not cease to value honesty because we recognize that lying to save an innocent life is sometimes morally right. We do not abandon the prohibition against theft because we understand that stealing bread to feed a starving child is not the moral equivalent of armed robbery. The taboo against cannibalism serves essential social functions in ordinary life: it reinforces respect for persons, discourages instrumentalization of human beings, and provides a bright line that upholds human dignity. None of these functions is undermined by recognizing that when a person faces death and the only tissue available is already-someone-else's, the dignity of the living takes precedence.

Moreover, the taboo against cannibalism, like all taboos, is not an end in itself. It is a means of protecting human dignity, preventing harm, and sustaining social trust. When the conditions that justify the taboo are absent — when no one is harmed, when the dead are treated with reverence rather than contempt, when the act serves the preservation of life rather than the destruction of it — then the moral foundation that supports the taboo is not undermined but honored. The taboo exists to protect human beings. Permitting survival cannibalism protects human beings. The principle serves the purpose.

VII. The Argument from Consistency

A particularly powerful argument for the moral permissibility of survival cannibalism comes from examining the inconsistencies in how we treat analogous situations. Modern medicine routinely uses products derived from human tissue for life-saving purposes. Cadaveric skin grafts are used to treat burn victims. Human-derived medical products — from dural grafts to heart valves made from human tissue — are implanted into living patients. We do not call these procedures cannibalism, but this is largely a matter of framing and familiarity. The physical reality is that human tissue is introduced into a living body for the purpose of sustaining or improving life.

If we accept — as nearly everyone does — that using deceased human tissue for transplantation is not only permissible but admirable, then we are already committed to the moral principle that dead human bodies can and should serve the living. Survival cannibalism is a more direct, less technologically mediated version of this same principle. The moral logic that makes organ donation heroic is precisely the logic that makes survival cannibalism defensible. To condemn the latter while celebrating the latter is to be guided not by moral principle but by squeamishness — and squeamishness, however understandable, is not an ethical argument.

VIII. Addressing the "Slippery Slope" Objection

Critics may object that even narrow justifications for cannibalism create a slippery slope: if we permit it in extreme survival situations, we open the door to permitting it in less extreme situations, then in recreational or cultural contexts, and eventually the entire prohibition collapses.

This objection conflacts recognition of an exception with erosion of a principle. Every moral right has boundaries, and the existence of boundaries does not mean they will be transgressed. We recognize self-defense as an exception to the prohibition against killing, but this recognition has not led to a general acceptance of violence. We recognize lying to save lives as an exception against the prohibition of dishonesty, but this has not destroyed the value of truth-telling. Moral boundaries are maintained not by pretending that no exceptions exist but by being rigorous about the conditions that permit them. The conditions outlined in this essay — death of the consumed, certainty of death without the act, absence of alternatives, and last-resort status — are strict enough to prevent any meaningful slope. They define a space so narrow and so extreme that it cannot plausibly be expanded to justify non-survival cannibalism.

Conclusion

The argument for the moral justification of cannibalism in extreme survival situations is not an argument for casual disregard of the sanctity of human life or human remains. It is, paradoxically, an argument rooted in precisely those values. The reason we revere the human body is because it houses, expresses, and enacts human life. When life has departed, the body remains worthy of respect — but the respect we owe it is not greater than the respect we owe to living persons facing annihilation.

In the starkest possible terms: if you are going to die, and the only thing that can prevent your death is tissue from someone who has already died, then choosing life is not a moral failing. It is a moral affirmation — a declaration that human life retains its value even in the most desperate, most degraded, most horrifying circumstances that existence can produce. The survivors of the Andes crash, the Donner Party, and countless other tragedies did not fail morally when they made their terrible choice. They honored the deepest moral commitments we hold: that life matters, that the dead are not harmed by serving the living, and that no abstract principle should require a human being to die when life can be preserved without causing harm.

Moral philosophy, at its best, does not flinch from hard cases. It does not allow the comfort of absolute prohibitions to substitute for genuine ethical reasoning. And when we reason carefully, honestly, and with full awareness of the gravity of what we are considering, the conclusion is clear: in the narrowest of circumstances, under the strictest of conditions, survival cannibalism is not morally wrong. It is — in the most tragic and profound sense — the right thing to do.

They want a world where:

  • No one ever has to make an impossible decision
  • No one ever has to choose between two bad options

But the world is not neat. It is not tidy. It is not predictable. Sometimes the plane crashes. Sometimes the ship sinks. Sometimes the storm doesn’t pass. And sometimes, the only thing standing between you and death is a terrible choice and a very sharp knife.

The Last Taboo: Rethinking the One Absolute We Can No Longer Afford

Ladies and gentlemen, colleagues, fellow human beings—

The Test of Consistency

Every moral framework we claim to hold is tested not in comfort, but in extremity. We say human life is sacred—yet we cage that sacredness between lines drawn by circumstance. But what happens when circumstance removes every other option?

Consider: we accept that a surgeon may amputate a limb to save a life. We accept that soldiers kill to defend their nations. We accept that parents may sacrifice their own well-being—their own organs, their own futures—for their children. In every case, we permit tremendous harm because the alternative is irreversible, absolute loss—death.

So I ask: if the harm caused by an act is weighed against death itself, and death is the worst outcome available, on what consistent moral ground do we condemn the act?

The Reality We Refuse to Name

  • The survivors of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571, 1972
  • Sailors of the Essex, devoured by the sea and desperation

In each case, rational, good people made an impossible choice: consume the dead to keep the living alive. And historically, we have shown them grace. Courts have declined to prosecute. Juries have wept. The community has judged them not as monsters, but as survivors of a hell none of us can fully imagine.

And here is what strikes me: mercy shown in individual cases must eventually become principle, or it was never mercy at all—it was sentiment.

I am not advocating cannibalism as lifestyle, as cuisine, or as cultural practice. I am arguing for the moral permissibility of consuming the remains of the already-deceased to prevent additional deaths when:

  1. All other sources of sustenance are genuinely exhausted
  2. No rescue is imminent
  3. The deceased did not object prior to death (or expressed willingness)
  4. The act preserves innocent life that would otherwise be inevitably lost

This is not permission. This is permission structure — the recognition that in the most extreme corners of human experience, our survival instinct and our moral duty to preserve life may align in a way that breaks one of our deepest taboos.

The Philosophical Core

The philosopher who argues for the inviolability of any act must answer this question: Is your rule worth a human life?

If a rule, applied consistently, results in the preventable death of a living, breathing person with hopes, with people who love them, with contributions yet unmade—then that rule must justify itself against their death.

Most absolutist positions cannot survive this accounting. The sanctity of the body after death is a profound value. I do not deny it.

But here is what I put against it: a living heartbeat. A child's next breath. A person's remaining years.

And when the choice is between those things and the disturbance of remains that will, in time, return to earth regardless—I contend that life carries the greater moral weight.

The Case From Empathy

If your sister were dying of starvation on a mountainside, and the only thing standing between her and death were the remains of someone who had already perished, would you let her die to preserve your moral comfort?

Would you tell her, with her body failing, that the rule was more important than her survival?

I suspect not. And if not for her, then on what grounds do we deny it to strangers? If the act is permissible in the imagination, it must be permissible in reality.

Reclaiming Honesty

We are, among other things, honest creatures—or we should be. And honesty demands we acknowledge that the taboo against cannibalism serves primarily as prevention of murder and exploitation. That is its true, noble purpose. Its function is to say: do not kill to consume.

But when death has already occurred independently—when the deceased is already gone—the taboo's protective function does not apply. What remains is simply revulsion. And revulsion alone has never been a reliable moral compass.

We were revolted, once, by the idea of blood transfusion. By open-heart surgery. By organ donation itself—the "desecration" of the body to save another. We learned to see past our instincts because the moral calculus demanded it.

I ask only that we apply the same rigorous reasoning here.

Conclusion

I am not asking you to like this argument. I am asking you to weigh it—against real lives, real survival emergencies, and the silence of loved ones who might have lived had we not been too afraid to acknowledge what is already, quietly, morally recognized.

We owe the survivors of extreme circumstances more than whispered gratitude that it was them and not us. We owe them a framework. A recognition. The acknowledgment that choosing life—even through unimaginable means—is not depravity.

Sometimes, it is the most human choice there is.

The Last Resort: A Moral Defense of Survival Cannibalism

The prospect of cannibalism invokes an immediate, visceral revulsion in the human psyche. It is perhaps the strongest of all cultural taboos, a boundary that separates "civilization" from "savagery." However, moral philosophy is not merely the study of comfortable norms; it is the rigorous examination of ethical principles under pressure. In such rare, catastrophic scenarios, cannibalism is not only morally permissible but can be argued as a moral imperative grounded in the supreme value of life, the hierarchy of ethical duties, and the absence of malicious intent.

The Primacy of the Right to Life

The foundational argument for the moral justification of survival cannibalism rests on the hierarchy of human rights, specifically the primacy of the right to life. Most ethical frameworks, from secular humanism to natural law theory, posit that life is the precondition for all other rights and values. Without life, there is no autonomy, no dignity, no future, and no capacity for moral agency.

In a standard societal context, the prohibition against cannibalism protects bodily integrity and human dignity. However, in a survival scenario—such as being stranded in the Andes after a plane crash, as in the 1972 Uruguayan rugby team disaster, or trapped in a lifeboat with no resources—the threat is not to dignity, but to existence itself. When the choice is binary—starve to death or consume the deceased to survive—the ethical weight shifts. To choose death when life is attainable through the consumption of already deceased tissue is to negate the very value that ethics seeks to preserve. If the ultimate moral good is the preservation of life, then the act that secures life, however repugnant, becomes morally justified by its outcome.

Distinction Between Murder and Survival

A critical distinction must be made between homicidal cannibalism (killing to eat) and survival cannibalism (eating those who have already died or whose death is inevitable and unrelated to the act of consumption). The moral outrage associated with cannibalism is largely tied to the violation of consent and the act of murder. In the specific scenario outlined—where cannibalism is the only means to sustain life—it is presupposed that the individuals consumed are already deceased or beyond saving.

Philosophers like Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, proponents of utilitarianism, would argue that the morality of an action is determined by its consequences. In this context, the "harm" caused to the deceased is negligible compared to the "good" of preserving the lives of the survivors. The deceased no longer possess interests, desires, or the capacity for suffering. The survivors, however, possess a profound interest in continuing to live. Therefore, the net utility favors survival. The act does not violate the rights of the deceased in a meaningful moral sense because rights are generally predicated on the existence of a subject who can claim them. Once life has ceased, the bodily remains become a resource, albeit a sacred one, rather than a person.

The Absence of Malice and the Role of Necessity

Moral culpability is deeply tied to intent. In criminal law and moral philosophy, the concept of necessity serves as a defense when an individual commits an otherwise wrongful act to prevent a greater harm. The cannibal in a survival situation acts not out of malice, greed, or deviance, but out of a biological and psychological drive for self-preservation. This lack of malicious intent strips the act of its typical moral stain.

Furthermore, the concept of "implied consent" can be invoked. Many ethical theorists argue that rational agents, if placed in the same hypothetical situation, would consent to their bodies being used to save the lives of others. This is akin to the logic behind organ donation after death, though far more extreme. In the absence of explicit consent, we can look to communal survival ethics: in a group facing extinction, the collective interest in survival overrides individual post-mortem bodily autonomy. The act is not a violation of the social contract but a desperate adherence to the most fundamental clause of that contract: the preservation of the community’s existence.

Psychological Trauma Does Not Equal Moral Wrong

Critics often argue that cannibalism causes profound psychological trauma to survivors, suggesting that the act is inherently harmful. However, the presence of trauma does not equate to moral wrongness. Soldiers experience trauma from killing in just wars; doctors experience distress from triage decisions where they must let some patients die to save others. The psychological burden is a testament to the gravity of the situation, not evidence of immorality. In fact, the reluctance and horror felt by survivors underscore their moral integrity. They do not enjoy the act; they endure it. This endurance, driven by the will to live, is a testament to the resilience of the human spirit rather than a moral failing.

Conclusion

To argue for the moral justification of cannibalism in extreme survival situations is not to endorse the practice lightly or to diminish the sanctity of the human body. Rather, it is to acknowledge the limits of abstract moral rules when confronted with the raw reality of existence. When death is certain without action, and the only alternative is the consumption of human flesh, the moral imperative shifts from preserving taboos to preserving life.

In these harrowing circumstances, the act is devoid of malice, grounded in the necessity of survival, and aligned with the highest ethical principle: the preservation of life itself. To condemn such acts is to prioritize symbolic purity over actual existence. Therefore, in the narrowest, most desperate confines of unavoidable survival, cannibalism is not a moral crime, but a tragic, justified, and deeply human response to the edge of oblivion.

A critical ethical distinction is made between killing for consumption and consuming the already dead. Most ethical defenses of survival cannibalism strictly limit permissibility to cases where:

This distinction preserves the sanctity of life (no murder occurred) while acknowledging the practical reality of survival. In some theoretical and real-world scenarios (e.g., mountaineering expeditions or military units), individuals may enter into pre-consent agreements regarding what should happen to their bodies if they die in a survival situation.

Paradoxically, in some group survival narratives, the shared burden of making such a difficult decision can reinforce group cohesion and shared purpose.

Accepting cannibalism as ethically permissible in desperate survival scenarios is not about redefining morality in normal times, but about recognizing the limits of ethical rules under extreme duress. The supposed "benefit" is purely instrumental: the preservation of human life when all other avenues have failed. It reflects a tragic ethical calculus where the violation of a profound taboo is weighed against the absolute value of survival, and in the most extreme cases, survival is deemed the greater good.

This perspective remains highly controversial and is not accepted in most legal systems (where necessity is rarely a full defense for homicide, though it may mitigate sentencing).
